title: Theorem
body_md: There exist infinitely many closed symplectic four-manifolds admitting the structure of hyperbolic $\pi$-orbifold.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: Of course, this does not rule out the possibility that some $\tilde{X}$ is indeed symplectic, or more generally has a non-vanishing Seiberg-Witten invariant for some other spin$^c$ structure; we will leave it as a interesting open question to determine the latter in full generality (including higher dimensional moduli spaces). For some examples of infinite families of hyperbolic four-manifolds tasselated by right-angled $120$-cells with vanishing Seiberg-Witten invariants, see \cite{BFS}.

title: Proposition
body_md: The branched covering is regular (i.e. for every $p,q \in N$ with $h(p)=h(q)$ there is a PL homeomorphism $\varphi \colon N \to N$ with $\varphi(p)=q$ and $h\circ \varphi = h$).
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: We have $h(p)=h(q)$ if and only if $p \in P_v$ and $q \in P_w$ correspond to the same point in $P$ and $v-w \in \ker f$. The automorphism $\varphi$ that acts as $\varphi\colon P_u \to P_{u-v+w}$ via the identity map sends $p$ to $q$ and we get $h\circ \varphi = h$.
head: environment

title: Example
body_md:
Let $P'$ be obtained from $P$ by merging some pairs of facets:
some examples are in Figure \ref{merge:fig}. Let $\lambda'$ be any colouring in $V'$ for $P'$. We construct a colouring $\lambda$ in $V = V'\times \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$ for $P$ simply by assigning the vectors $(\lambda(F),0)$ and $(\lambda(F),1)$ arbitrarily to the two facets of $P$ that are merged in the facet $F$ of $P'$. We get a degree 2 branched covering $N \to N'$, whose ramification locus is the codimension-two submanifold that is the preimage of the merging locus. 

The two examples in Figure \ref{merge:fig} are particularly interesting because in both cases $P$ and $P'$ can be given a right-angled hyperbolic and flat structure, respectively. Therefore we get a hyperbolic 2- or 3-manifold $N$ that is a double branched covering over a flat 2- or 3-manifold $N'$. The ramification locus consists of some points and some closed geodesics, respectively. The 3-dimensional example is a variation of a well-known construction of Thurston.
In both examples, by interpreting $P'$ as a hyperbolic right-angled $P$, we assign a hyperbolic $\pi$-orbifold structure to $N'$. 

Our main goal is now to construct some similar 4-dimensional examples.

\label{isotropyprop}
    The ramification locus of the branched covering $\tilde{M} \to \Sigma \times \Sigma$ is a 2-dimensional subspace, {which consists of simple, triple, and nodal points only}.

title: Proof
body_md: The ramification locus is the union of all the merging loci of all the products $D_1 \times D_2$ in the decomposition. The points in $R\cap B$ and $s(R) \cap s(B)$ give rise to nodes. The valence 3 vertices of the circles with 5 prongs form some closed curves entirely made of triple points. All the rest of the ramification locus consists of simple points.

label: 80tori
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{80tori}
    The ramification locus of the four-fold branched cover $p\colon M \to \Sigma \times \Sigma$ {consists of simple and nodal points}. It is the union of 80 homologically non-trivial product tori that intersect transversely in 160 nodal points. Each torus intersect four other tori at a single point, and we can orient the tori so that the intersections are all positive for the product orientation on $\Sigma\times \Sigma$.

title: Proposition
body_md:
The ramification locus of the double branched cover $\tilde{M} \to M$ consists of 160 orientable surfaces of genus 2 and 40 of genus 3, all with trivial normal bundle. 
    
    By interpreting $P'$ as a right-angled hyperbolic 120-cell $P''$ {with merged facets}, we assign to $M$ the structure of a hyperbolic $\pi$-orbifold {with singular set the ramification locus. The singular set} consists of totally geodesic surfaces.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The merging locus of $P'$ consists of the green faces $f_1,f_2,f_3$ shown in Figure \ref{dodecaedri3:fig}-(left), repeated in each prism. Figure \ref{dodecaedri3:fig}-(right) shows the colours of the edges of $f_1,f_2,f_3$ induced from $\lambda$. By what said in Section \ref{submanifolds:subsubsection} the preimage of $f_i$ in $\tilde{M}$ consists of some copies of the surface $S_i$ obtained from the pentagon $f_i$ equipped with the induced colouring in $V/V_i$, where $V = (\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^7$ and $V_i$ is the subspace generated by the colourings of the two facets containing $f_i$. We have
    $$V_1 = V_2 = {\rm Span} (e_1+e_5, e_1+e_5+e_7), \quad V_3 = {\rm Span} (e_1, e_1+e_7)$$
    In $V/V_1 = V/V_2$ the pentagons $f_1$ and $f_2$ are coloured with 3 independent vectors, hence $S_1=S_2$ is tessellated into $2^3=8$ pentagons, hence $\chi(S_1)=\chi(S_2)=-2$ and $S_1,S_2$ are orientable surfaces of genus 2. In $V/V_3$ the pentagon $f_3$ is coloured with 4 independent vectors and hence $\chi(S_3)=-4$ and $S_3$ in an orientable surface of genus 3. 
    
    Every pentagon $f_1,f_2$ gives rise to $2^{5-3}=4$ surfaces of genus two, while each $f_3$ gives rise to $2^{5-4}=2$ surface of genus three. Since there are 20 prisms and hence 20 pentagons of each type, we get $20\times 2\times 4 = 160$ surfaces of genus two and $20 \times 2 = 40$ surfaces of genus three.
